title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
book_title: Inside the ₹100 Economics and the 326-Day Inventory Chain

epigraph.quote: Vertical integration lowers your unit cost per tablet, but every extra stage of chemistry adds weeks to your working capital cycle.
epigraph.author: Supply Chain Economics Maxim

web_blocks.html: Aurobindo Pharma runs a global network of 25+ manufacturing plants [5]. Its Indian campuses in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh span APIs, oral solids, sterile injectables, biologics, and the 15,000 MTPA Kakinada Pen-G hub [5][10]. Overseas sites include New Jersey and Dayton in the US, Puerto Rico, and a >2-billion-unit plant in China (~$145 million capex) [16][22]. Producing most of its own APIs lets Aurobindo capture dual margins and shield finished-dose lines from spot shortages [4][5].

Distribution channels vary sharply by region. In the United States, three wholesalers dominate: McKesson, Cencora, and Cardinal Health [22]. Aurobindo also serves retail chains and hospital Group Purchasing Organizations (GPOs) for Eugia's injectables [12][22]. Concentrated buyers hold strong pricing power and cause order swings, such as early FY26 wholesaler destocking [2][22]. In Europe, local arms like Arrow (France) and Puren (Germany) sell directly to community pharmacies and regional hospital tenders [13]. That direct model requires higher local stock, yet it yields stickier pricing and 23%+ revenue growth [2][15]. In ARV, sales flow through multi-year Global Fund and PEPFAR tenders [6].

web_blocks.caption: FY26 Consolidated Unit Economics Waterfall (INR Crore & Per ₹100 Revenue)
web_blocks.takeaway: Out of every ₹100 of FY26 revenue, ₹79.59 went to operating costs (including ~₹4.60 in R&D), leaving ₹20.41 in EBITDA, ₹10.41 in Net Profit, ₹16.42 in CFO, and ₹7.33 in Free Cash Flow after ₹9.09 of heavy growth capex [1][2][6].

web_blocks.html: The main yellow flag in Aurobindo's unit economics is Inventory Days. It climbed from 239 days in FY15 to 284 days in FY24, 295 days in FY25, and 326 days in FY26 [1]. Nearly 11 months of raw-material cost now sit on the balance sheet [1]. Three forces drive this bloat. First, vertical API-to-tablet chains hold work-in-progress across multiple steps. Second, direct European pharmacy sales require local safety stock across seven nations [2]. Third, new plants in Kakinada, China, and Dayton pre-built inventory ahead of sales [10][16]. So far, Aurobindo offset this by stretching Days Payable from 117 days in FY25 to 151 days in FY26, keeping Working Capital Days at 44 [1]. If supplier credit tightens before inventory turns improve, working capital will absorb cash.

web_blocks.title: Hidden Unit-Economics Drag: Remediation & Underutilized Fixed Assets
paragraphs: FY26 operating expenses absorbed three temporary drags. First, Eugia Unit III and Unit I incurred remediation consultant fees and extra batch-testing costs [4][8][9]. Second, Pen-G Kakinada posted early ramp-up losses until turning EBITDA-positive late in Q4 FY26 [2]. Third, the China oral-solids plant ran at a pre-break-even loss [16]. As these assets scale in FY27, EBITDA conversion should rise—provided no USFDA import alert freezes finished stock.

book_paragraphs: To see how Aurobindo's business model converts chemistry into cash, let's put ₹100 of FY26 revenue on the table and trace every rupee. Out of ₹33,653 crore in sales, raw materials and intermediates take ₹30.62, employee salaries across 25-plus global plants and R&D labs take ₹15.42, and other operating costs—power, freight, roughly ₹4.60 of R&D, and FDA remediation consultants—take ₹33.54. That leaves ₹20.41 in operating EBITDA.

From that ₹20.41, depreciation takes ₹5.28—a number that is climbing steadily as billions of rupees in Pen-G, China, and biologics construction move from work-in-progress onto the active asset register. Interest takes just ₹1.14, offset almost entirely by ₹1.20 of treasury income on Aurobindo's ₹10,676 crore cash pile. After ₹4.78 in taxes, you and I are left with ₹10.41 in net profit. Even better, because depreciation is a non-cash charge and working-capital payables expanded, operating cash flow came in at ₹16.42 per ₹100 of sales, leaving ₹7.33 in free cash flow even after spending ₹9.09 on heavy growth capex.

Now here is the operational catch you cannot ignore: inventory days hit 326 in FY26, up from 239 days in FY15 and 295 days in FY25. Think about what 326 inventory days means in plain English—nearly eleven months of cost of goods sitting in fermentation vats, port warehouses, and European distribution depots. In a vertical model that stretches from Penicillin-G fermentation in Kakinada to pharmacy shelves in Paris and wholesaler cages in New Jersey, long inventory cycles are partly structural. Still, Aurobindo kept its net working capital at 44 days in FY26 only because it stretched supplier payables from 117 days to 151 days.

That trade-off—bloated inventory financed by extended payables—works smoothly when demand is growing and plants are FDA-compliant. If a sterile plant gets hit with an import alert, however, finished vials sit stranded on the balance sheet while suppliers still demand payment. That is why distribution velocity and regulatory compliance are inseparable in this business.

Let's also examine the geographic contrast inside Aurobindo's 25-plus manufacturing plants. In India, massive oral-solid and API complexes across Telangana and Andhra Pradesh—culminating in the 15,000-tonne Kakinada fermentation hub—give Aurobindo unmatched unit-cost scale for tablets, capsules, and beta-lactam antibiotics. In the United States, facilities in New Jersey and Dayton, Ohio provide local-for-local manufacturing for controlled substances and sensitive launches that benefit from Made-in-USA supply security. And in China, Aurobindo's ~$145 million oral-solids facility (with capacity exceeding two billion units) gives it direct access to China's volume-based procurement tenders while diversifying export capacity.

Why does this sprawling footprint weigh on unit economics during ramp-up years? Because pharmaceutical plants carry heavy fixed-cost validation before a single commercial rupee is booked. Throughout FY26, Aurobindo's P&L absorbed three simultaneous drags: pre-break-even operating losses at the China facility, initial fermentation ramp-up costs at Kakinada (which only reached EBITDA break-even toward the end of Q4 FY26), and third-party consultant and batch-testing expenses at Eugia's Hyderabad sterile sites. As Kakinada scales from 40%–50% utilization toward 10,000+ tonnes annualized and China reaches EBITDA break-even, those fixed-cost absorption drags should gradually flip into operating leverage.

Still, you and I must keep a sharp eye on the cash conversion cycle. In FY15, Aurobindo held 239 days of inventory, 107 days of receivables, and 136 days of payables—a net cash conversion cycle of 210 days. By FY26, receivables improved to 77 days, but inventory stretched to 326 days and payables expanded to 151 days, leaving the cash conversion cycle at 252 days (and Screener's working capital days at 44). That means Aurobindo's ₹5,526 crore of FY26 operating cash flow was helped by stretching supplier credit. Over the next two years, durable cash quality requires inventory days to fall back below 275 rather than relying on ever-longer payable terms.

Let's walk through the unit economics of a single ₹100 of Aurobindo's FY26 revenue as if we were sitting on the factory floor in Hyderabad. Out of every ₹100 in sales, roughly ₹30.62 goes to raw materials and intermediates—an unusually lean number for a generic drugmaker, made possible only because Aurobindo synthesizes so many of its own APIs in-house. Another ₹15.42 pays the global workforce of scientists, plant operators, and European commercial teams, while ₹33.55 covers power, freight, R&D (around 4.5% to 4.7% of sales), and regulatory compliance. That leaves ₹20.41 in operating EBITDA before ₹5.28 of depreciation, ₹1.14 of interest, ₹1.20 of other income, and ₹4.78 of taxes bring net profit to ₹10.41.

Now here is the catch that every serious owner must respect: turning ₹10.41 of accounting profit into ₹16.42 of operating cash flow in FY26 required a massive working-capital balancing act. Aurobindo carried 326 days of inventory—nearly eleven months of raw materials, work-in-process, and finished goods—alongside 68 days of customer receivables. How did net working capital still stay at a manageable 44 days? Because Aurobindo stretched supplier payables to 151 days, effectively using vendor credit to finance part of its global buffer stock.

Think about why that 326-day inventory number matters so much for your capital-efficiency checklist. Holding nearly a year's worth of inventory across 150 countries protects fill rates when Red Sea shipping lanes or Chinese API ports clog up, which wins preferred-supplier status with US and European hospital buyers. Yet it also locks up thousands of crores of cash on the balance sheet and leaves the company exposed if sterile batches face FDA hold-ups or generic prices reset faster than stock turns over.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Aurobindo's ₹100 unit economics show a resilient 20.4% operating margin and healthy free cash flow, but the 326-day inventory cycle is a reminder that backward integration is capital-hungry. Watch whether inventory turns improve as Pen-G and China hit steady-state utilization.
